title: Organizing the band in 1917 and the Cave, Forest Grill and Cobb's years
summary: DeDroit organized his band in 1917, was hired by Mr. Grunewald for the Cave and Forest Grill, then spent seven years at Cobb's and recorded for OKeh. He describes the Dixieland and show-tune repertoire and his side jobs.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: I organized my band in 1917. The play at a hotel in Atlantic City. When the war came on, the contract was cancelled. So I played a little jazz at the Orphan Theater, and Mr. Grunlong happened to be in the audience, and he heard us. He waited for me, and he said, they tell me you have a band. I said, yes. He said, could I hear it? I said, let's play him. So we made an audition. We played two numbers. He okayed the orchestra, sent us to get uniforms, and we stayed with him four solid years in the cave and in the forest grill. Forest Grill was on Barone Street. The cave was under the Roosevelt. Then the Roosevelt was then called the Grunlong. We finished at the Grunlong, now the Roosevelt, on the 19th of March and opened at Cobb's Restaurant on St. Charles Street on the 21st. One day, because Mr. Cobb had been after me for a couple of years, we stayed with Mr. Cobb seven years. And like all good things, let's come to an end. During the period at Cobb, we made records for the Oak Cave phonograph company. The personnel of the orchestra changed from time to time, as it does with all bands, but I managed to give them the kind of music they want. And then, we had a good job. Our strong point was good Dixieland, clean Dixieland, and show tunes. Because having had good musicians, we could play anything. And we had the best people in the town, and some of them liked good music now and then. Through that engagement, I signed a five-year contract with O.K. O.K. went on for business, so I had made a few dollars on the record, so I didn't worry about it. In addition to that, Mr. Cobb gave me the music for the luncheon period, the dinner period, and I had the dance man. In addition to that, I was finishing the music at three Morrisons cafeterias. Strange to say they had music. As soon as AFSCAP demanded a license for every seat, they cut out the music.
No, that's progress. Now what, now what, you can't shut it off now? That's the first answer.
